articles.snippet: Fractile Secures £577M Series C to Scale AI Chip Production n24.com.tr
articles.text:

Fractile Secures £577M Series C to Scale AI Chip Production
Fractile has raised £577 million in Series C funding as the London-based chipmaker prepares to deploy its inference hardware in data centers by 2027.
Elena Whitmore
·
30 October 2026 09:45
·
2 min read
·
14,436 reads
Google'a Ekle
Fractile , the London-based artificial intelligence hardware startup, has secured £577 million in a Series C funding round. Official filings at Companies House confirm the capital injection, marking the firm's largest fundraising effort to date.
Strategic Capital Allocation
The funding was executed through nine share allotment returns filed between 15 October and 28 October. The breakdown of the equity classes includes:
Series C-1: £147.8 million
Series C-2: £37.4 million
Series C-3: £392.2 million
The allotments reflect a significant valuation surge for the company, which was in discussions earlier this year for a pre-money valuation of approximately $6.5 billion. The total raise, when converted, equates to roughly $774 million.
Hardware Ambitions
Founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin and Yuhang Song , Fractile specializes in inference chips designed to accelerate the response times of large AI models. The company aims to reduce the time required for complex AI workloads from one month to a single day by keeping data adjacent to processing transistors.
Market demand is currently driven by a severe scarcity of high-performance compute hardware. Anthropic has already signaled its intent to integrate Fractile technology, placing an initial order valued at $250 million. The hardware is slated for deployment in 2027.
The Road to 2027
Despite the substantial capital backing, the company faces a critical test. Fractile has yet to ship a production-ready chip to customers. The firm previously utilized its Series B funds to establish engineering operations in London , Bristol , San Francisco , and Taipei . The current infusion of cash provides the runway necessary to transition from design to mass manufacturing.
Investors are betting on the firm's architecture to outperform existing solutions. Competition is fierce. Cerebras and Etched have set high benchmarks for valuation in the inference space. Success hinges on Fractile hitting its 2027 delivery targets. The market is watching. The hardware must perform.

articles.title: Harvey raises $550M at $15.5B valuation
articles.text:
← Deals

Harvey raises $550M in funding round, valuation reaches $15.5B
SaasRise • Oct 1, 2026
Type Venture Funding - Growth Stage
Value $550M
Harvey Company
Legal AI startup Harvey closed a $550 million growth‑stage round on Oct. 1, 2026, pushing its post‑money valuation to $15.5 billion. The capital will fund product acceleration and deeper market penetration as AI‑driven legal tech adoption spikes among law firms.
Harvey announced a $550 million financing on Oct. 1, 2026, valuing the legal‑AI platform at $15.5 billion post‑money. The round, the largest for the company to date, comes as its annual recurring revenue (ARR) sits at $400 million, implying a roughly 14× ARR multiple on the new valuation. ## Deal Terms The funding round was led by a syndicate of venture firms (details were not disclosed) and will be deployed to expand Harvey’s product suite, scale its engineering team, and accelerate go‑to‑market efforts in North America and Europe. The infusion follows a broader surge of capital into AI‑centric SaaS businesses, underscoring investor confidence in the legal‑tech vertical’s growth trajectory. ## Market Context Recent ILTA survey data show that 40 % of law firms prioritized generative AI over any other technology in the past year, with cloud SaaS applications trailing at 25 %. Within that AI landscape, Microsoft Copilot leads usage at 76 % of firms, while Harvey is adopted by 43 % of respondents, ranking just behind Copilot, Claude (44 %), and Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44 %). Token consumption on Harvey’s platform has risen 14‑fold in the last six months, reflecting both deeper integration into legal workflows and the looming shift from subscription‑based pricing to consumption‑based models. The funding positions Harvey to double‑down on its open‑weight model strategy, compete directly with the newly launched OpenAI Astra for Law and Google Gemini Enterprise for Legal, and potentially lock in enterprise contracts before the market pivots to token‑based pricing. As law firms grapple with legacy on‑prem accounting systems—still present in 52 % of firms—the move toward cloud‑native, AI‑enhanced solutions like Harvey could accelerate the displacement of traditional software stacks, reshaping the competitive dynamics of the legal‑tech ecosystem.
Why It Matters
Harvey’s fresh war‑chest enables it to outpace rivals in product velocity, particularly against Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude, which currently dominate law‑firm AI usage. By expanding its model‑training capabilities and bolstering its token‑pricing infrastructure, Harvey can lock in higher‑margin consumption revenue, pressuring competitors that remain tied to subscription models. For Thomson Reuters, which is investing $40 million in its own legal LLM, Harvey’s scale and market share intensify the race for data‑rich, open‑weight models, likely prompting faster feature roll‑outs and pricing adjustments across the sector.
For investors, the deal validates the premium placed on AI‑enabled SaaS platforms that address high‑touch, regulated verticals. The 14× ARR multiple signals that capital markets are willing to bet on deep‑stack AI integration as a defensible moat, setting a benchmark for future legal‑tech valuations and influencing fund allocation toward similar vertical AI plays.
Key Points
Harvey raised $550 million, lifting its valuation to $15.5 billion.
Post‑money ARR stands at $400 million, implying roughly a 14× ARR multiple.

articles.snippet: Five robotics startups raise $510M as investors chase physical AI Dealroom
articles.text:
Fundraise Oct 14, 2026, 22:43 UTC
Five robotics startups raise $510M as investors chase physical AI
What's the deal? Five robotics startups — ICON , Mecka AI , MMI , Multiply Labs , and Ultra — raised a combined $510 million in the week of October 12, spanning construction, surgery, data training, drug manufacturing, and warehouse automation.
The biggest round: ICON, which builds 3D-printing construction robots, raised a $200 million Series D co-led by Baillie Gifford and funds managed by BlackRock . It plans to build a new R&D center, develop new construction systems, and expand its US footprint.
ICON has worked with the Department of War since 2020 on military housing and public infrastructure. It has won more than $370 million in government contracts and built more than 270 homes.
Who else raised? MMI, which makes robotic tools for micro- and supermicro surgery, secured a $125 million Series D led by BioStar Capital Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → . It has deployed nearly 50 of its Symani systems worldwide, used in more than 3,500 surgeries, and will fund US expansion.
Multiply Labs raised a $75 million Series B led by NantWorks for robots that manufacture cell and gene therapies. It sells systems directly to customers, letting them own their supply chain in a heavily regulated industry.
Mecka AI, which builds hardware and sensors to collect egocentric data for training robots, raised a $60 million Series B led by Sequoia . That came four months after $60 million across two undisclosed rounds in June. The company says it is on track for $300 million in run-rate revenue by year-end, after crossing $100 million in June.
Ultra closed a $50 million Series A for two-armed warehouse robots that pack and sort orders. Unlike its peers, Ultra leases hardware monthly, with software supplied through a partnership with Physical Intelligence .
Why now? Training data is in high demand among investors, and specialised robots — for surgery, drug manufacturing, and construction — are moving from labs into regulated real-world use.
The signal: The week's deals skipped general-purpose humanoids entirely, a reminder that capital is flowing across the full robotics stack — from data pipelines to task-specific machines — not just the flashiest category.

articles.title: Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal
articles.snippet: Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal The Robot Report
articles.text:
Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal
By Eugene Demaitre | October 30, 2026
Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics
Humanoid robotics developers continue to raise millions of dollars. Agility Robotics Inc. and Churchill Capital Corp XI today said that they expect Agility to raise about $465 million in its proposed merger with the special-purpose acquisition company, or SPAC.
According to Agility, the gross capital raise includes:
About $164 million from Churchill XI’s trust account
Approximately $201 million from a common stock PIPE (private investment in public equity) committed at $10 per share, led by Foxconn with participation from existing and new institutional investors
$100 million of equity funding already received following the announcement of the business combination
That total is less than the $620 million that Agility predicted at a $2.5 billion valuation when it first announced the planned business combination in June. The Robot Report has reached out to the company for comment and will add it if we get a response.
“Agility is expected to enter the public markets well capitalized to execute its planned investments in commercial expansion and support growing customer demand,” stated the Salem, Ore.-based company .
Agility expects to close the SPAC transaction, subject to shareholder approval and the customary closing conditions, on Nov. 4. The company has claimed that it will be the first U.S. publicly traded, pure-play humanoid supplier with commercial deployments.
Agility gets Digit ready for customers
Last month, Agility unveiled its Digit 5 humanoid, which had new legs (and possibly wheels ) and is designed to work safely alongside people and support a range of workflows. Last week, Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer, and Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at the company, spoke about humanoid advances at RoboBusiness 2026.
Agility this month also chose Nyobolt for fast recharging, which it said will enable its robots to operate for more than 20 hours a day.
The company said it is “on track to begin deliveries to early-access customers in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of 2027.” Agility also said it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5.
Humanoid use cases are growing
Digit continues to make progress in live operations. In a September S-4 statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Agility reported $1.8 million in net sales in 2025. Its customers across nine sites include Toyota , Mercado Libre , and Schaeffler .
AGCO this month announced plans to deploy Digit in its agricultural machinery factory in Kansas.
And this week, Agility said it is expanding its partnership with GXO Logistics, implementing humanoids in North Carolina and Tennessee.
Humanoid companies continue fundraising, acquisitions
Agility’s investors include NVIDIA (with whom it also expanded its relationship), Amazon, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Schaeffler, Foxconn, Abico, DCVC, and Playground Global. The company said that all existing shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company and will be subject to a 180-day lock-up at closing.
Some of the top funding rounds for humanoid companies so far this year include Neura Robotics ‘ $1.4 billion Series C, XPeng Robotics ‘ $900 million Series A, AI 2 Robotics ‘ $735 million Series C, and Apptronik ‘s $520 mill
